title: Switzerland Announces Plan to “Legalize” Cannabis, Again.
description: A committee of the Swiss House of Representatives has introduced a bill to legalize recreational cannabis “in an effort to curb the illegal market....
content_html_sanitized:
A committee of the Swiss House of Representatives has introduced a bill to legalize recreational cannabis “in an effort to curb the illegal market.”

 

Unfortunately, it will not do that because it will create a state controlled monopoly that will leave plenty of room for the black market because of high taxes and arbitrary controls.

 

Also, taxes would be based on the level of THC, with products having higher levels of THC to be taxed more. Oh, perfecto! So black market weed will be better than the state monopoly stuff.

 

The revenue from sales is supposedly going to fund “harm reduction, addiction services, and subsidies for health insurance cost savings.”

 

Meanwhile, back in the real world, adding insult to injury, this bill keeps cannabis classified as a “dangerous narcotic.” There’s nothing quite like insulting your customers to generate business.

 

Forgive my skepticism.  Indeed, the reason for saying that they are planning to legalize cannabis “again” is that at little over 24 years ago, on March 9, 2001, Reuters reported, “Swiss clear the way for cannabis legalisation

BERN, March 9, 2001 (Reuters) - “The Swiss government on Friday endorsed a draft law that would legalise the consumption of marijuana and hashish and allow a limited number of "dope shops."

The bill submitted to parliament seeks to bring Swiss law into line with the reality that one in four people aged 15-24 regularly gets high in the Alpine state, according to a poll commissioned last month by the Swiss government.”

So, over twenty years ago, the Swiss government said, "Decriminalising the consumption of cannabis and the acts leading up to this takes account of social reality and unburdens police and the courts.”


In late 2000, the “Swiss Federal Commission for Drug Issues”– made up of prominent people from the financial, medical, academic and law-enforcement worlds issued a report saying that cannabis policy must reflect prevailing moral values and attitudes to civil liberties. The report concluded that using criminal law to dictate the behavior of an individual user "is repugnant to the fundamental values of a legal system founded on personal liberties, and is therefore illegitimate".

From 2000: See Swiss Commission Denounces Marijuana Prosecutions As "An Arbitrary Act of Coercion".

 

So, I am not particularly excited about this latest Swiss flirtation with freedom. It may pass, but the Swiss people deserve better, and eventually they will get it.

 

How time flies! With or without a Swiss watch. Now, will someone please play the William Tell Overture!
